abstract: |
  We study whether Graph Neural Network (GNN) partial starts improve Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) for the Capacitated Facility Location (CFL) problem. We compare no external start, a start based on the root relaxation, and a neural start with matched assignment counts. On six easy instances at sixteen threads, the GNN-to-baseline time ratio is 0.843 for solver runtime and 1.046 for supervised execution with delimited cold preparation. In the twelve-hour comparison, the neural start reached the target sooner than the baseline on four of five thread settings for one medium instance, while another medium instance remained censored with the neural start at every setting. In a separate one-hour comparison across three solver seeds, the neural start alone attained the reported 0.01% gap on two of ten medium instances. One of those cases retains a numerical restriction. A separate training comparison yielded a 1.831-fold whole-job speedup with four graphics processing units, alongside lower selected predictive quality. The findings identify conditions under which partial starts can improve search and show how preparation cost and reuse affect their practical value.
---
# Introduction

Capacitated Facility Location (CFL) asks which facilities to open and how to serve customers within capacity at minimum cost. A Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver searches for feasible decisions and bounds their cost.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) can learn patterns in related instances and propose values for some binary decisions. These values are partial warm-start candidates: they need not form a complete or feasible solution. The solver attempts to complete them and may repair or reject them. Supplying a candidate leaves the original constraints and variable domains unchanged.

Prediction accuracy alone does not establish optimization benefit. A partial assignment that agrees with many reference labels may still be unhelpful to the search. Conversely, a small set of useful assignments may improve optimization without maximizing a classification score. Even an observed solver-level advantage may disappear once the cost of constructing the graph, obtaining features and evaluating the GNN is counted.

The research question is: Can partial initial values predicted by a graph neural network (GNN) be used as warm starts for a deterministic MILP solver and improve its performance when solving Capacitated Facility Location (CFL) problems? We operationalize this question by examining the conditions in which neural starting information helps or harms and the extent to which observed benefits remain within the measured computational costs. Determinism is conditional on the solver configuration and execution conditions; it is not a guarantee of identical endpoints under a wall-time limit.

We model, develop and evaluate a GNN in a high-performance computing environment to investigate these effects on MILPBench CFL instances [@milpbench]. The study makes two empirical contributions. First, it characterizes conditional optimization effects through comparisons of primal quality, dual bounds, gaps and time to quality targets across instances and thread configurations. Second, it assesses computational cost--benefit within explicit measurement boundaries, distinguishing solver time from preparation, reuse, amortization and training. The prediction-to-Start mechanism is the experimental method supporting these contributions, rather than a separate claim of algorithmic novelty.

# Related Work

## Learning to Optimize

Learning to Optimize uses learned information to assist decisions within an optimization process [@bengio2021; @chen2022primer]. The acceleration, estimation and adaptation perspectives reviewed by @chen2024tutorial help distinguish a proposal that changes search guidance from one that replaces the optimizer. Here the network proposes candidate binary values; the MILP solver retains responsibility for feasibility and optimality assessment.

The variable--constraint bipartite representation follows @gasse2019, whose network learns branching choices. We adapt the prediction target and solver interface rather than claiming a new graph representation. Graph-based combinatorial reasoning has a wider range of uses [@cappart2021], but a useful representation in one solver task does not by itself establish the value of a partial start in CFL.

## Learned primal guidance and partial starts

The closest precedents concern learned assignments and primal search. MIP-GNN already includes neural warm-starting [@khalil2022]. Neural Diving generates partial assignments and completes associated sub-MIPs [@nair2020], whereas Predict-and-Search explores regions around predictions [@han2023]. Prediction-guided neighbourhoods [@ding2020], local branching [@fischetti2003] and uncertainty-based reduction [@canturk2024] also use predicted structure to focus solution effort. These methods differ in what they predict and how they modify or restrict the search.

Native partial MIP starts offer a distinct interface. Selected values are supplied as a candidate, with other variables unspecified; the original feasible region remains available [@gurobi2026]. Learned constraints [@qu2026], starting scenarios for another optimization setting [@goerigk2025] and nonlinear solution-generation mechanisms [@tang2024l2o] illustrate other interfaces, rather than direct experimental comparators for the present CFL population. The broader branch-and-bound literature makes the same distinction between learned components and complete solution procedures [@scavuzzo2026survey].

Our comparison asks how the solver responds to no external start, an LP-ranked partial start and a GNN-ranked partial start. The latter two match their assignment and positive-value counts. This does not isolate the causal effect of class-aware ordering or establish a first GNN--MILP integration. Appendix A compares the interfaces. Direct cost comparisons would also need to match their preprocessing, training and search protocols.

## Performance and computational cost

An improvement depends on the endpoint being compared. Earlier attainment of a quality target, a better feasible objective and a smaller terminal gap answer different questions. Comparable models, settings, stopping rules and parameter selection are therefore central to computational evaluation [@beiranvand2017]. The same requirement applies to the cost boundary: shorter solver time need not imply a shorter application once neural preparation is included. We evaluate these boundaries on identified instances, without transferring improvement percentages from other problems or treating absent cost reporting as a universal literature gap.

# Methodology

## Optimization model and reference labels

A CFL model couples facility-opening and customer-service decisions through capacity and demand constraints. The experiments use the supplied benchmark models directly. Their general matrix representation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_p^\star&=\min_x\; c_p^\top x+c_{p,0},\\
A_px&\mathrel{\bowtie_p}b_p,\\
\ell_p\leq x&\leq u_p,\qquad x_j\in\mathbb Z\quad(j\in I_p).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $p$ identifies an original instance; $A_p,b_p$ and $\bowtie_p$ encode the rows and their senses, and $I_p$ identifies integer variables. This notation describes the model actually read by the software. We do not replace it with an alternative economic formulation whose column correspondence has not been established. Original coefficients, row senses, bounds, domains and objective constants are preserved. All experiments explicitly use MINIMIZE, overriding the MAXIMIZE declarations in the supplied files while retaining their original bytes as provenance.

For binary variables, labels come from checked reference incumbents. An incumbent is a feasible solution retained by the solver, subject to the stated numerical checks. Admission verifies variable coverage, bounds, integrality, linear constraints and objective reconstruction, and requires a finite reported relative gap no greater than 10%. Labels may therefore be approximate and need not identify an exact or unique optimum. Predicting their values is a supervised-learning task, not an optimality certificate.

## From the model to a bipartite graph

A variable is represented by a variable node and a linear constraint by a constraint node. An edge joins them when the variable has a nonzero coefficient in that row, and the coefficient is an edge feature. This representation gives the GNN access to the couplings present in the MILP.

The graph has seven variable channels (objective, bounds, type and stored root-relaxation value), five constraint channels (right-hand side and row sense) and one coefficient channel. Signed logarithms and clipping control the representation's range without changing solver coefficients. Appendix C specifies their order and transformations.

The relaxation values are captured during a separate preparation stage. Gurobi reads the original minimization model with Presolve=0, NodeLimit=1, one thread, seed 42 and a 600-second limit. At the first optimal MIPNODE event at the root, the callback reads cbGetNodeRel, stores the aligned vector and terminates preparation. This is not an independent call to model.relax(), nor necessarily the final root state after every cutting-plane pass.

## Predictor, training and validation

The Gasse-inspired network alternates constraint and variable updates. A constraint combines messages from its incident variables; a variable then receives information from its incident constraints, including the newly updated constraint state. The fitted configuration uses two propagation cycles and 32-dimensional embeddings, with 26,753 trainable parameters. Each direction has separate message and update perceptrons with a ReLU hidden activation. Messages are summed and normalized with fixed statistics fitted on training graphs. The final head produces binary-variable logits $s_j$ and sigmoid scores $q_j=\sigma(s_j)$.

This is one fixed architecture, not the result of a comparative architecture search. Its typed propagation is appropriate to the variable--constraint representation. Two cycles and modest width define the evaluated capacity; their numerical values are not claimed to be optimal. Appendix A gives the equations and distinguishes this implementation from the upstream branching network and other GNN families.

Training minimizes positive-class-weighted binary cross-entropy,

$$
\ell_j=-w_+y_j\log\sigma(s_j)-(1-y_j)\log(1-\sigma(s_j)),
$$

with $w_+$ equal to the negative-to-positive target ratio in training data. The weighting gives rare positive labels greater influence. It also means that sigmoid scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities [@gneiting2007].

Adam uses learning rate 0.001 [@kingma2015], with gradient-norm clipping at 1 [@pascanu2013]. These references motivate an optimizer and a stabilization operation, not CFL-specific optimality of the fixed values. The historical serial path uses one graph per update, four balanced draws per training instance per epoch and a ceiling of 100 epochs. Minimum validation weighted BCE selects the checkpoint; maximum pooled validation F1 selects the threshold. The retained CPU threshold is 0.9991843104362488. Fixed settings, training-fitted quantities and validation-selected choices are distinguished in Appendix C.

## Inference, partial starts and the three methods

At application, the stored root vector is aligned with the original variables, encoded with model features and assembled into the graph. The frozen GNN is loaded in evaluation mode and produces scores without gradient computation. Reference labels used by a separate feasibility audit do not enter the neural forward or assignment selection.

For $n$ eligible binary variables, the requested support budget is

$$K=\min\{n,20000,\max(1,\lfloor0.10n\rfloor)\}.$$

GNN-START (G) selects predicted ones first, ranked by their scores, and fills remaining places with confident predicted zeros. Variable names break ties. If no one is predicted, the policy abstains. The 20,000-value cap binds on medium instances, so their actual coverage is below 10%.

RELAX (R) ranks the stored LP values instead. If G supplies $k$ assignments including $q$ ones, R assigns one to the $q$ highest clipped LP values and zero to the $k-q$ lowest remaining values. It chooses its own indices. R is not an independent LP-only heuristic: its support and one count depend on G, and that dependency is included in preparation accounting. BASE (B) supplies no external start; the solver's internal heuristics remain available.

Each method uses a fresh copy of the same model. Selected values enter the Start attribute; other variables remain GRB.UNDEFINED. No original bound is fixed. Gurobi attempts to complete or repair the candidate and may reject it. Start submission, loading, first feasible incumbent and final performance are distinct observations. Mathematical signatures check preservation of the objective, rows and bounds.

@fig-pipeline summarizes the offline learning and application stages. The detailed R/G matching rules and a schematic example are in Appendix A.

![Learning a predictor and supplying candidate information to an unchanged MILP. R matches G's assignment count k and positive count q.](figures/figure_pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline width=87% fig-pos="!htbp"}

The frozen predictor and validation-selected rule transfer to application. Preparation supplies aligned model/root information; it does not transfer the new instance's solution. All methods retain the original feasible region.

# Experimental Design

## Instances, partitions and comparison populations {#sec-populations}

The benchmark contains 90 candidates divided equally among easy, medium and hard categories. Quality screening admits 54: 30 easy and 24 medium, with no hard instance admitted. The fixed learning split is 34 training, ten validation and ten predictive-test instances. @tbl-populations separates the populations that answer different parts of the research question.

| Evidence | Instances and design | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Predictor fitting and selection | 34 train / 10 validation / 10 predictive test | Quality-selected labels; fixed original-instance roles |
| Principal CPU comparison | Six easy, four medium; five thread caps; seed 42 | 150 observations; ten exposed instances |
| One-hour solver-seed comparison | Six easy, ten medium; one thread; seeds 42–44 | 144 runs paired by instance and seed |
| Preliminary CPU study | Six medium test and six validation instances | Separate historical protocol |
| Matched GPU training | One versus four GPUs; same split | One matched-work pair |

: Populations and purposes of the reported comparisons. {#tbl-populations}

The instance is the comparison unit. Binary targets, methods, thread caps and seeds supply measurements within it. The predictive tests and principal CPU instances were historically exposed. The historical optimization test and the 12-hour CPU campaign retain their own populations and clocks, as detailed in Appendix B.

## Solver protocols and repeatability

The principal CPU comparison uses physical thread caps 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, seed 42, a 3,600-second solver limit and MIPGap=0.0001 (0.01%). B/R/G share the model and parameter map, apart from their supplied starts; predictor, root vectors and starts remain fixed across caps. The longer-horizon protocol specifies 43,200 seconds. The preliminary six-medium study and root preparation retain separate configurations (Appendix C).

Gurobi is designed for deterministic search under controlled inputs, version and hardware, including conventional parallel MIP [@gurobideterminism2025]. Changing Threads changes the configuration, not a random replicate. Conventional parallel MIP differs from Concurrent MIP, which runs independent searches and can be nondeterministic. Its effective setting was not exported. Seed 42 holds one search perturbation fixed; it does not control changes in models, starts or execution conditions.

Method=-1 delegates continuous/root algorithm selection to Gurobi; Method=1 explicitly requests dual simplex. Automatic selection commonly chooses dual simplex for MIP roots, and may choose deterministic concurrent methods for larger roots [@gurobi2026]. Neither an actual root algorithm nor an undocumented parameter value is inferred from a default.

TimeLimit can interrupt otherwise repeatable search at different amounts of work as machine conditions vary. WorkLimit instead limits algorithmic work under otherwise deterministic conditions; its units are not universal seconds [@gurobiwork2026]. It is a different budget, not a replacement for the adopted protocol. The separate solver-seed comparison keeps one physical thread, the 3,600-second solver limit and fixed starts, and rotates method order within each instance across seeds 42, 43 and 44. These seeds perturb search with the same predictor. Appendix C details the execution and measurement conditions.

## Endpoints and comparison rules {#sec-metrics}

For minimization, a checked feasible incumbent supplies an upper bound $z^P$, while a valid dual bound $z^D$ describes what may still be achievable. For finite nonzero $z^P$, relative gap is $g=|z^P-z^D|/|z^P|$. Zero or unavailable values retain their explicit states. A smaller gap can reflect primal improvement, dual progress or both; it is not synonymous with a better incumbent.

We distinguish terminal primal, dual and gap, reported terminal-target attainment, and first observed time to a common quality threshold. A target that is unobserved during adequate follow-up is right-censored, not attained at the time limit. Missing observations and numerical restrictions are separate from censoring. Callback times are observed crossing times, not exact continuous first hits. A run may reach 10% gap yet remain censored for the much tighter terminal criterion.

Speedup divides reference time by comparison time for comparable work and termination. For B versus G or R versus G at an eligible common target, $T_B/T_G$ or $T_R/T_G$ above one favours G. The reciprocal cost ratio $T_G/T_B$ favours G below one. Within-method strong scaling holds the problem fixed and varies resources. For a thread cap $r$ relative to one, speedup is $T_m(1)/T_m(r)$ and parallel efficiency divides it by $r$. This uses the configured cap, whereas CPU utilization requires a separate measurement. Censored runs contribute coverage without observed time ratios.

The comparisons are descriptive. For the solver-seed comparison, we pair by instance and seed, take the latest observation at or before 3,600 seconds, and use the terminal point when the solve ends earlier. We summarize seed contrasts within each instance before comparing across instances. The 48 blocks comprise repeated observations of 16 instances. Archive intervals for the retrospective comparison are exploratory.

Predictive metrics measure reference-label agreement separately. Precision is TP/(TP+FP), recall is TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is their harmonic mean. Average precision (AP) is the noninterpolated sum of precision weighted by recall increments, following @sklearnap; it differs from trapezoidal PR-AUC. Rare-positive assessment uses precision--recall measures alongside ROC-AUC [@saito2015]. The Brier score averages squared score error [@brier1950]. Expected calibration error (ECE) uses ten equal-width positive-score bins [@guo2017]. Variable-pooled metrics combine targets; parent-macro metrics average the individually computed instance values.

## Preparation, execution and resource costs

Computational performance includes attained solution quality, native solver Runtime, application elapsed time and memory. The application clock may include root capture, construction and transfer of inputs, model loading, inference and Start integration [@silva2025pascal]. The supervised attempt includes recorded process overhead. Preparation intervals are charged once, including R's dependence on G for matching. Training, queueing and orchestration have separate clocks.

Cold-use and amortization calculations are scenarios, not independent end-to-end trials; missing components remain unavailable. Seven-use and five-use allocations are distinct assumptions. Campaign accounting counts shared work once, rather than summing alternative method scenarios as repeated expenditure.

UJA's dgx-dasci inventory lists eight 32-GB V100 GPUs, two 20-core CPUs and 512 GB of memory. It is not a runtime hardware probe or an allocation of all eight GPUs. The 6 Gb/s interface is an inventory specification. Appendix C separates requested, allocated and measured resources.

# Computational Results

## Predictive quality of the fixed model

The archived predictive test contains 5,536,400 binary targets with 5,265 positives (approximately 0.0951%). Its pooled F1 is 0.6993 and parent-macro F1 is 0.7027; precision and recall are 0.6923 and 0.7064. AP is 0.7745, distinct from trapezoidal PR-AUC 0.7747. These results characterize the predictor, without establishing the utility of its selected starts.

Validation loss selects historical epoch 34 rather than the terminal epoch 100. Appendix B reports the original loss curves and predictive table, together with their separate archive provenance. The later GPU comparison uses a different global update schedule and does not replace the CPU checkpoint.

## Conditional optimization effects {#sec-mvp2-current}

The principal analysis has 150 seed42 observations on ten instances. Ninety observations concern six easy instances and sixty concern four medium instances. Appendix B gives all reported dispositions and per-instance outcomes; the sensitive M4/M12 observations remain part of the same sample.

The geometric-mean time ratios in @tbl-principal-ratios summarize paired relative effects on the six easy instances. For example, G/B is $\exp\{\frac{1}{6}\sum_i\log(T_{G,i}/T_{B,i})\}$. Each instance has equal weight regardless of its absolute runtime. This is a multiplicative summary, not a ratio of total computing times or evidence of uniform acceleration.

{{< include tables/principal_ratios.qmd >}}

All 90 easy observations attain the reported 0.01% gap criterion, permitting descriptive time comparisons. Their final gaps are not uniformly zero: @tbl-easy-gaps reports the largest final gap for each instance/method across the five caps. Appendix B provides every final gap and runtime. These are tolerance-based outcomes, rather than exact-optimum certificates.

{{< include tables/principal_easy_gaps.qmd >}}

@fig-principal-time shows individual paired behaviour and separate CPU scaling.

![Between-method time ratios and within-method CPU scaling on the six easy instances.](figures/figure_principal_time_scaling.pdf){#fig-principal-time width=100%}

The left panel shows G/B and G/R solver-time ratios by instance and cap, with geometric means. Lower ratios favour G. The right panel shows each method's geometric-mean scaling relative to its own one-thread runtime. No panel is a population-level uncertainty estimate.


G is slower than B in aggregate at one/two threads and faster at four/eight/sixteen; G/R also varies. Individual effects differ, and the exploratory sixteen-thread G/B interval includes one. These summaries establish neither an optimal cap nor a statistical interaction. More threads do not ensure acceleration: B/R geometric-mean scaling is below one at caps four through sixteen, and G's improvement is nonmonotonic.

The medium-instance comparisons concern terminal quality as well as censored times. @fig-medium-gap retains each instance separately, including the numerically sensitive cases.

![Terminal reported relative gaps for the four medium instances across B/R/G and thread caps.](figures/figure_principal_medium_gap.pdf){#fig-medium-gap width=100%}

Panels show terminal observations, not values measured at an identical exact horizon. Open markers indicate censoring for the terminal target. M4/M12 panels retain their numerical restrictions; a displayed zero is not an exact optimality certificate.

On medium instance 0 at one thread, G improves the primal (4.6556 versus B's 4.6664) but weakens the dual (4.3230 versus 4.3504), leaving a larger terminal gap. On medium instance 7 at eight threads, G's much better primal (5.4337 versus 10.7283) yields a smaller gap despite a weaker dual (4.7261 versus 4.7750). Appendix B retains all configurations and adverse outcomes. Primal and dual changes therefore require joint interpretation.

Medium instance 0 with G at sixteen threads reports zero terminal gap after approximately 3204 seconds, while both comparators are censored for the terminal target. This is a solver-reported outcome under tolerances, not an exact certificate. M4 and M12 retain metric-specific numerical limits: acceptance of original floating-point vectors does not establish feasibility of rounded diagnostic copies. Their observations cannot be promoted to certified speedups.

## Long-horizon CPU observations {#sec-cpu-long-partial}

The long-horizon evaluation retains M0, M4, M7 and M12, their original starts, seed 42 and five thread caps, with a 43,200-second solver limit. All 60 configurations were completed and reconciled. Forty-seven reached the reported 0.01% criterion and 13 were time-limited, all on M7. These results are analyzed separately from the 150-observation retrospective comparison; thread caps are not independent replications.

On M0, G reached the target before B at four of five caps, but was slower than both comparators at two threads. All 15 M7 runs ended with the same reported primal value, 5.428377599678637; their terminal gaps therefore differ through their dual bounds. Only B at one thread and R at sixteen threads closed the terminal gap. At eight threads, R ended at 1.653% and G at 1.838%; at sixteen, G remained at 1.448%. Earlier intermediate progress does not imply terminal attainment or uniform dominance. Retaining M7 preserves this adverse regime: a timeout is not evidence of infeasibility.

On M12 at eight and sixteen threads, G finished much earlier than B and R. All three reported zero internal gap, but G reported a slightly higher objective. The exact primal audit established feasibility for three stored G points. Seven examined control points contained a tolerated fractional binary, and their rounded patterns cannot satisfy an original linking constraint for any continuous completion. The reported times do not establish certified speedups or a common optimum. M4 retains its separate restriction. Appendix B gives the complete records and audit.

## Efficiency after preparation costs {#sec-cost-results}

A solver-level advantage is not necessarily an application-level advantage. @tbl-principal-costs compares five already documented cost boundaries for the six easy instances at sixteen threads.

{{< include tables/principal_costs.qmd >}}

The solver-only G/B ratio of 0.8435 becomes 1.0461 with delimited cold preparation, or 1.0692 with broader allocation. The corresponding seven-use scenarios yield 0.8935 and 0.8969. Accounting scope and reuse thus reverse the direction of the estimate.

These are conditional cost scenarios, not complete deployment measurements. The exploratory intervals around the sixteen-thread solver and cold-use ratios both include one. The observation is useful for accounting decisions on this sample, without establishing a universal break-even rule. It also does not remove preparation from the measured campaign expenditure or imply that missing operational costs are zero.

## Complementary matched GPU training {#sec-gpu-matched}

The matched seed 42 pair compares serial one-V100 training with four-V100 distributed data parallel (DDP) training. Serial denotes one training process; it does not imply sequential arithmetic within the GPU. DDP replicates the model across processes and synchronizes their gradients [@li2020ddp]. Both arms use the same learning split, train-fitted initialization and global batch of four. Each update averages four graph losses: accumulated serially in one arm, one per rank in the other. Both complete 100 epochs, 13,600 graph presentations and 3,400 updates. Validation selects checkpoints independently.

| Measure | Serial 1 V100 | DDP 4 V100s |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Physical CPU cores |4|16|
| Training loop (s) |1724.128|795.637|
| Slurm job elapsed (s) |2021|1104|
| Assigned GPU-hours |0.5614|1.2267|
| Selected epoch |99|92|
| Minimum validation BCE |0.045286|0.048772|
| Selected parent-macro F1 |0.723065|0.690597|
| Selected parent-macro PR-AUC |0.783809|0.769959|

: Timing, selected predictive quality and allocated resources for one matched training pair. {#tbl-gpu-pair}

Loop speedup is 2.167 with 54.17% efficiency; whole-job speedup is 1.831. Assigned GPU-hours increase. Selected F1 falls 0.032468 (3.247 percentage points), exceeding the predeclared descriptive 0.02 loss margin; PR-AUC falls 0.013850. The smaller PR-AUC loss does not establish preserved predictive quality or statistical noninferiority. @fig-gpu-bce shows the unmodified loss trajectories.

![Training and validation weighted BCE for the matched serial/distributed comparison.](figures/gpu_bce_by_epoch_article_en.pdf){#fig-gpu-bce width=90% fig-pos="!htbp"}

Communication and gradient synchronization can contribute to sublinear DDP speedup [@li2020ddp]. GNN workloads can also involve irregular data movement [@zheng2020distdgl]; here each rank processes complete instance graphs. Matched global batches do not establish identical floating-point trajectories [@pytorch21numerical]. CPU and GPU allocations change together. The single pair shows an F1 loss, but does not identify its cause. These weights do not replace the CPU predictor.

## One-hour paired solver-seed comparison {#sec-pr94-results}

All 144 runs yielded terminal records. On the six easy instances, every method attained the observed 0.01% gap in all 18 instance–seed pairs. At that target, geometric mean time ratios R/B, G/B and G/R were 1.038, 1.083 and 1.043, respectively. G was faster than B in ten of the 18 pairs, but the larger slowdowns on F0 and F29 raised the geometric mean.

For the ten medium instances, B, R and G attained a 10% gap in 9, 8 and 12 of 30 runs per method, respectively. At 0.01%, only G attained the target, on M12 and M20 across all three seeds. M12 remains numerically restricted. Across the eight medium instances outside M4 and M12, the median of the instance-level paired gap differences was -2.11 percentage points for G versus B and -2.52 for G versus R. These fixed-budget differences include censored runs with observed incumbents and bounds. Appendix B details the pair counts, numerical restrictions and supervised costs.

The separate historical six-medium comparison is reported in Appendix B. It uses its own cohort, worker clock and seed-42 protocol.

# Discussion

Label agreement describes the predictions. Their effect on the MILP depends on the solver's completion, incumbent use and remaining search. The easy-instance ratios change direction across thread caps, and the medium results show that primal gains can coexist with weaker dual progress. The usefulness of a Start therefore depends on the quality target and budget as well as on predictive accuracy.

The unchanged feasible region distinguishes these starts from the restricted searches of Neural Diving, Predict-and-Search and uncertainty-based reductions [@nair2020; @han2023; @canturk2024]. Following the warm-start precedent of MIP-GNN [@khalil2022], our contribution is a conditional CFL assessment, not evidence of superiority over those algorithms.

R controls assignment counts and class composition but depends on G's preparation and supplies different indices and values. Their contrast therefore concerns the complete starting information; identifying the causal effect of prioritizing ones would require a controlled ablation.

At sixteen threads, the easy-instance solver estimate favours G, whereas cold-use scenarios do not; reuse changes that conclusion. Likewise, shorter GPU training accompanies lower F1 and higher allocated GPU-hours. These outcomes describe distinct trade-offs.

Quality-selected labels, prior exposure and small cohorts constrain generalization. The one-hour study varies solver seeds with fixed starts and predictor weights. Wall-time stopping and resource conditions may contribute to the observed heterogeneity. M4 and M12 retain their numerical restrictions.

# Conclusions and Future Research

We compared GNN-generated partial starts with unguided and relaxation-ranked starts on CFL while preserving the original feasible region. Benefits depend on instance, thread cap, quality target and cost boundary; stronger primal values need not yield stronger dual bounds. The retrospective, preliminary and long-horizon studies retain separate populations and support conditional rather than universal conclusions.

Solver gains can disappear with cold preparation, while reuse changes their economics. Faster distributed training can also reduce selected predictive quality and increase allocated GPU-hours. The accounting remains delimited rather than a complete deployment estimate.

Across three solver seeds, G's earlier progress on some easy runs did not consistently carry through to the tight target. The one-hour medium comparison shows better reported gaps on most instances and an instance-specific attainment advantage on M20 outside the numerically restricted cases. Work-based stopping, root-method contrasts, neural hyperparameters, retraining and mechanism ablations remain future research.

Data and code availability. The [project repository](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/cfl-gurobi-gnn) provides code, partitions, derived outcomes and scripts for tables and figures. Original models are obtained from MILPBench. Access to intermediate data and checkpoint bytes depends on their artifact-specific availability and redistribution terms. Appendix C identifies which steps can be reproduced from public material.
